analysis.one_liner: Expands workplace discrimination and harassment protections and phases out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 senators including the committee chair, was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in November 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strengthen federal protections against workplace discrimination and harassment. It would make clear that discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, and pregnancy is sex discrimination under the Civil Rights Act, cover every employer no matter how small, and extend protections to contractors, interns, and volunteers. It would create a statutory definition of workplace harassment, ban forced arbitration and gag clauses in discrimination cases, give low-income workers grants for legal help, and phase the tipped minimum wage up to the full federal minimum wage so servers keep their tips on top of a real wage.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — including contractors, interns, and volunteers who are largely unprotected today — would gain new legal rights, longer deadlines to sue, and access to lawyers paid through grants. The roughly several million tipped workers paid a federal base wage of $2.13 an hour would see that base rise in annual steps until it equals the full federal minimum wage, with a guaranteed right to keep their tips. Workers in states without their own stronger protections benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing harassment and tipped employees

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth, related medical conditions, and sex stereotypes as explicitly protected categories under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and lowers the employer coverage threshold from 15 employees to 1.
Extends anti-discrimination protections to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees, who are generally outside current employment law coverage.

Writes a statutory definition of workplace harassment under which a single incident can qualify, incidents are judged in total rather than one by one, and a victim need not show physical or psychological injury.

Prohibits employers from requiring workers to sign predispute arbitration agreements or nondisclosure clauses covering discrimination and harassment claims, so cases can go to court and be discussed publicly.
Phases the tipped minimum wage up in annual increments until it equals the federal minimum wage for other workers, and gives employees a statutory right to retain their tips.
Extends the time limits for filing discrimination complaints, including for federal employees, and makes compensatory and punitive damages available without the current caps tied to employer size.
Creates grant programs for legal assistance to low-income workers facing employment discrimination and for state-based workers' rights advocacy systems.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the costs: restaurants would eventually owe the full minimum wage before tips on every server, employers using forced arbitration and nondisclosure agreements would lose those tools in discrimination cases, and all covered employers would face new policy, training, and posting requirements with fines of $1,000 to $5,000 per violation. Businesses would also face broader litigation exposure as damages caps come off and more workers gain the right to sue.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers must adopt comprehensive nondiscrimination policies, conduct training, and post them, with fines of up to $1,000 per offense and at least $5,000 for repeated or willful violations; Title VII coverage would extend to employers with as few as one employee.

The bill removes the statutory caps on compensatory and punitive damages and lowers the proof standard to a 'motivating factor' test, which would raise the cost and volume of employment litigation for employers of every size.
The bill bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a claim or defense in Title VII cases, removing an exemption that religious employers and their advocates have sought.
Phasing out the tip credit raises menu-priced labor costs for restaurants, which commonly operate on thin margins, and the bill offers no offsetting adjustment for those businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core gains are real and broadly shared: clearer legal rights against harassment and discrimination for nearly all workers, the end of a federal base wage of $2.13 an hour for tipped staff, and the removal of forced arbitration in these cases. The costs fall on employers, mainly restaurants and businesses that rely on arbitration clauses, and the expanded damages and relaxed proof standards would predictably increase litigation. Those are tradeoffs, not design flaws, though a skeptic could fairly argue the litigation expansion reaches further than the harassment problem it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 17, 2021, read twice, and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee — whose chair was the bill's own sponsor — and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill with 21 original cosponsors: 20 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 1 of its 2 independents.
The Senate referred the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction, and no further action appears in the record.
No Republican senator cosponsored the bill.
The bill died in committee at the end of the 117th Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced new harassment liability, the loss of forced arbitration and nondisclosure agreements, and the full minimum wage for tipped staff are better off because the bill never moved. Tipped workers remain at a $2.13 federal base wage, and contractors, interns, and volunteers remain outside federal anti-discrimination coverage.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington and Chair, Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which was read twice and referred to her own committee; the committee never scheduled action on it.

against.name: 50 of 100 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independents; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding 50 of 100 seats the bill had no realistic path to the floor even if it had cleared committee.

industries.note: The bill phases out the sub-minimum tipped wage, which today lets these employers pay a federal base of $2.13 an hour and count tips toward the minimum, and it targets harassment of tipped employees directly. Eliminating the tip credit transfers wage costs from workers and taxpayers to restaurant payrolls.

industries.industry: Employers using mandatory arbitration and nondisclosure agreements
industries.note: The bill bans predispute arbitration agreements and certain nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses in discrimination and harassment matters, ending the practice of resolving these claims privately. The cost to employers is losing a shield from public court cases; the gain to workers is access to a judge and public record.

Covered employers gain model policies, training materials, and technical assistance from the EEOC, including materials tailored to businesses with fewer than 15 employees, but they face mandatory policy and training duties with per-violation fines. Extending Title VII coverage to one-employee businesses spreads the compliance burden to the smallest firms.
